queue.title: The feedback you can survive
queue.description: Asking for feedback can be a sophisticated form of avoidance. Founders unconsciously pick the people, questions, and framing that can't return a no — and call it research.
queue.linkedinTeaser:
You did the work — talked to ten people, took notes. And somehow every conversation left the idea exactly as intact as it started. That's not luck. You chose feedback you could survive.

When you're attached to an idea, you ask the people most likely to be kind, the questions least likely to find the soft spot, in a framing that already assumes you're right. It feels like research. It's built so it can't return a no.

The tell: if your research never changes your mind, you're not testing — you're collecting reassurance.

What's the one question about your idea you've been avoiding?

queue.title: Go looking for the no
queue.description: If you can't validate yourself, encouragement isn't a verdict, and you quietly pick the feedback you can survive — the move that's left is the uncomfortable one: go looking for the no.
queue.linkedinTeaser:
Most founders seek validation and merely tolerate criticism. Flip it: go looking for the no.

If your idea has a fatal flaw, it exists right now whether you've found it or not. You can pay to discover it today — one hard question, a little discomfort — or in twelve months, after the build and the launch. Same flaw, very different invoice.

A no isn't a verdict on you. It tells you which part is wrong — market, timing, price — early, while changing course is cheap. A no in July is often what makes a yes in October possible.

The mirror always says go. The door might say no. Walk up to it hoping it tells you the truth.
